subject: Physics
prerequisite: Newton's Laws of Motion, Weight and Gravity
content: FORCE FIELDS AND GRAVITATIONAL FIELDS. A force field is a region of space in which an object experiences a non-contact force. Force fields are represented by vectors showing the direction of the force, and by field-line diagrams where the spacing between lines indicates the strength of the force: closer lines mean a stronger force. A gravitational field is a force field in which objects that have mass experience an attractive force. Every mass creates a gravitational field around itself. Gravity is always attractive and never repulsive. TYPES OF GRAVITATIONAL FIELD. A uniform gravitational field exerts the same gravitational force at every point, represented by parallel, equally-spaced field lines all pointing in the same direction. Near the Earth's surface the field is treated as approximately uniform. A radial gravitational field has field lines pointing towards the central mass from all directions; as distance from the centre increases the field lines spread out, indicating decreasing force. The Earth's field is radial when considered on a large scale. GRAVITATIONAL FIELD STRENGTH. Gravitational field strength g is the gravitational force per unit mass at a point. Its unit is newtons per kilogram (N per kg), equivalent to metres per second squared. Formula: g equals F divided by m, where F is the gravitational force in newtons and m is the mass in kilograms. In a uniform field g is constant. In a radial field g decreases with distance from the source. On the Earth's surface g is approximately 9.81 N per kg. The weight of an object is given by: Weight (F) equals m times g, confirming that weight depends on both mass and the local gravitational field strength. Because g is the acceleration due to gravity, objects near the Earth's surface accelerate at approximately 9.81 metres per second squared when in free fall.

subject: Physics
prerequisite: Gravitational field strength, Newton's second and third laws
content: NEWTON'S LAW OF UNIVERSAL GRAVITATION. Gravity acts on any objects that have mass and is always attractive. Newton's law of gravitation states that the gravitational force between two masses is directly proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres. Formula: F equals G times m1 times m2 divided by r squared, where G is the gravitational constant equal to 6.67 times 10 to the power negative 11 newton metres squared per kilogram squared, m1 and m2 are the two masses in kilograms, and r is the distance between the centres of the masses in metres. The force obeys an inverse-square law: doubling the separation reduces the force to one quarter of its original value. Both masses experience equal and opposite forces (Newton's third law). WEIGHING THE EARTH. Newton realised gravity keeps the Moon in orbit. By equating the gravitational force on the Moon to the centripetal force required for circular orbit, and using the known orbital radius (3.84 times 10 to the power 8 metres) and orbital period (2.36 times 10 to the power 6 seconds), we can calculate the mass of the Earth. Gravitational force equals centripetal force gives: G times mE times mM divided by r squared equals mM times v squared divided by r, which simplifies to: mE equals r times v squared divided by G, giving mE approximately equal to 6.01 times 10 to the power 24 kilograms. WORKED EXAMPLE. Calculate the gravitational force between two neutrons in the Crab Nebula separated by 2 metres, given the mass of a neutron is 1.67 times 10 to the power negative 27 kg. F equals G times m1 times m2 divided by r squared equals 6.67 times 10 to the power negative 11 times 1.67 times 10 to the power negative 27 times 1.67 times 10 to the power negative 27 divided by 2 squared equals 4.65 times 10 to the power negative 65 newtons.

subject: Physics
topic: 3. Gravitational Field Strength in a Radial Field
prerequisite: Newton's law of gravitation, gravitational field strength definition
content: GRAVITATIONAL FIELD STRENGTH IN A RADIAL FIELD. An example of a radial gravitational field is that formed by a point mass or a spherically symmetric body (such as the Earth or the Sun). In a radial field, the gravitational field strength g varies with the distance r from the centre of the mass. Derivation: The gravitational force on a mass m2 placed in the field of mass m1 is F equals G times m1 times m2 divided by r squared. Gravitational field strength is defined as g equals F divided by m2. Combining these: g equals G times m1 divided by r squared. Written more generally: g equals G times M divided by r squared, where M is the mass of the object creating the field, G is the gravitational constant, and r is the distance from the centre of the mass. This shows that g is inversely proportional to r squared, so doubling the distance from the centre of a mass reduces g to one quarter of its original value. The gravitational field strength at the Earth's surface can be calculated using the Earth's mass (6.01 times 10 to the power 24 kg) and radius (6.4 times 10 to the power 6 m), giving g approximately equal to 9.81 N per kg. For a geostationary satellite orbiting at height h equals 35800 km above the Earth's surface, the distance from the Earth's centre is r equals R plus h equals 42200 km equals 4.22 times 10 to the power 7 metres, giving g equals 0.23 N per kg at that orbit.

subject: Physics
prerequisite: Gravitational field strength, work done and energy
content: GRAVITATIONAL POTENTIAL. Gravitational potential V at a point is defined as the work done per unit mass when moving an object from infinity to that point. Gravitational potential at infinity is defined as zero. As an object moves from infinity to a point in a gravitational field, energy is released (the gravitational potential energy decreases), so gravitational potential is always negative or zero. Formula for gravitational potential in a radial field: V equals negative G times M divided by r, where G is the gravitational constant, M is the mass of the body creating the field in kilograms, and r is the distance from the centre of the mass in metres. The unit of gravitational potential is joules per kilogram (J per kg). GRAVITATIONAL POTENTIAL DIFFERENCE. The gravitational potential difference delta V between two points is the energy per unit mass needed to move an object between those two points. The work done when moving a mass m between two points with potential difference delta V is: Work done equals m times delta V. The gravitational field strength g is related to the gravitational potential by: g equals negative dV divided by dx, where dV divided by dx is the gradient of the potential-distance graph. For small distances: g times delta x equals negative delta V. GRAVITATIONAL POTENTIAL AT GEOSTATIONARY ORBIT. V at geostationary orbit (r = 4.22 times 10 to the power 7 m) equals negative G times M divided by r equals negative 6.67 times 10 to the power negative 11 times 6.02 times 10 to the power 24 divided by 4.22 times 10 to the power 7 equals negative 9.52 megajoules per kilogram.

subject: Physics
prerequisite: Coulomb's law, electric fields and electric potential (Topic 6A)
content: COMPARING ELECTRIC AND GRAVITATIONAL FIELDS. Electric and gravitational fields share mathematical similarities because they both follow an inverse-square law for force. SIMILARITIES: Both forces follow an inverse-square law (F is proportional to 1 divided by r squared). Both fields can be uniform or radial. Both use field lines to represent the field. The equations have the same mathematical form: Gravitational force: F equals G times m1 times m2 divided by r squared; Electrostatic force: F equals k times q1 times q2 divided by r squared. Gravitational field strength: g equals G times M divided by r squared; Electric field strength: E equals k times Q divided by r squared. Gravitational potential: V equals negative G times M divided by r; Electric potential: V equals k times Q divided by r. DIFFERENCES: Gravity is always attractive, while the electrostatic force can be either attractive (opposite charges) or repulsive (like charges). Gravity acts on mass, while the electrostatic force acts on electric charge. The electromagnetic force is much stronger than gravity; the Coulomb constant k equals 9.0 times 10 to the power 9 newton metres squared per coulomb squared, while G equals only 6.67 times 10 to the power negative 11. A charged object can be shielded from an electric field (using a Faraday cage), but there is no way to shield a mass from a gravitational field. Gravitational potential is always negative; electric potential can be positive or negative depending on the sign of the charge creating the field.

subject: Physics
prerequisite: Circular motion, centripetal force, Newton's law of gravitation
keywords: T squared = (4pi squared / GM) times r cubed
content: ORBITAL MOTION AND KEPLER'S THIRD LAW. When an object orbits a mass, the gravitational force provides the centripetal force needed for circular motion. Equating centripetal force and gravitational force: m times v squared divided by r equals G times M times m divided by r squared. Simplifying: v squared equals G times M divided by r, showing that the orbital speed v is inversely proportional to the square root of r. DERIVING KEPLER'S THIRD LAW. Since velocity is the rate of change of displacement, for a circular orbit: v equals 2 pi r divided by T, where T is the orbital period. Squaring: v squared equals 4 pi squared r squared divided by T squared. Substituting into v squared equals G M divided by r: 4 pi squared r squared divided by T squared equals G M divided by r. Rearranging: T squared equals 4 pi squared divided by G M, times r cubed. This is Kepler's third law: T squared is directly proportional to r cubed. The constant of proportionality is 4 pi squared divided by G M, where M is the mass of the central body being orbited. For a circular orbit of the Moon (r = 3.84 times 10 to the power 8 m, T = 2.36 times 10 to the power 6 s): T squared divided by r cubed equals 4 pi squared divided by G M equals a constant, confirming Kepler's third law. ORBITAL SPEED. The orbital speed of a satellite is given by: v equals the square root of G M divided by r. A satellite in lower orbit moves faster than one in higher orbit. A geostationary satellite has an orbital period of 24 hours (86400 seconds), which fixes its orbital radius at approximately 42200 km from Earth's centre.

subject: Physics
topic: 7. Black Body Radiators and Radiation Curves
content: BLACK BODY RADIATORS AND RADIATION CURVES. A black body radiator is a theoretical object that is a perfect emitter and absorber of all possible wavelengths of electromagnetic radiation. In practice, a good approximation is an enclosure (cavity) with a small hole; radiation entering the hole bounces around inside and is absorbed with near-perfect efficiency. Stars behave approximately as black bodies. RADIATION CURVES. A radiation curve is a graph of intensity (power emitted per unit area per unit wavelength interval) against wavelength for radiation emitted by an object at a given temperature. Key features of black body radiation curves: The curve rises steeply from zero at very short wavelengths, reaches a maximum at the peak wavelength lambda max, then falls off gradually at longer wavelengths. The peak wavelength lambda max shifts to shorter wavelengths (higher frequencies) as temperature increases — this is Wien's displacement law. As temperature increases, the total area under the curve (total power emitted per unit area) increases greatly — this is described by the Stefan-Boltzmann law. The Sun (surface temperature approximately 5800 K) has its peak wavelength in the visible part of the spectrum, near 500 nanometres. Cooler stars (around 3000 K) appear red because their peak wavelength is in the infrared, and only the red end of the visible spectrum is significantly emitted. Hotter stars (around 15000 K) appear blue-white because their peak is in the ultraviolet and the blue end of the visible spectrum dominates.

subject: Physics
prerequisite: Black body radiation, luminosity, surface area of a sphere
keywords: L = sigma A T to power 4
content: THE STEFAN-BOLTZMANN LAW. Stefan's law (Stefan-Boltzmann law) states that the power output, also called luminosity L, of a black body radiator is directly proportional to its surface area A and to the fourth power of its absolute temperature T. Formula: L equals sigma times A times T to the power 4, where sigma (the Stefan-Boltzmann constant) equals 5.67 times 10 to the power negative 8 watts per metre squared per kelvin to the power 4 (W per m squared per K to the power 4), A is the surface area in metres squared, T is the absolute temperature in kelvin, and L is the luminosity (total power output) in watts. For a spherical star of radius r: L equals sigma times 4 pi r squared times T to the power 4. APPLICATIONS. The Stefan-Boltzmann law can be used to compare the properties of stars. A star with a larger surface area or higher temperature will have a greater luminosity. A bigger star at a lower temperature can have the same luminosity as a smaller, hotter star. WORKED EXAMPLE. The Sun has radius 7.0 times 10 to the power 8 metres and surface temperature 5800 K. Luminosity of the Sun: L equals sigma times 4 pi r squared times T to the power 4 equals 5.67 times 10 to the power negative 8 times 4 pi times (7.0 times 10 to the power 8) squared times 5800 to the power 4 equals 3.95 times 10 to the power 26 watts.

subject: Physics
prerequisite: Black body radiation curves, electromagnetic spectrum
content: WIEN'S DISPLACEMENT LAW. Wien's displacement law states that the peak wavelength lambda max of radiation emitted by a black body is inversely proportional to its absolute temperature T. The peak wavelength is the wavelength at which the radiation curve has its maximum intensity. Formula: lambda max times T equals a constant equal to 2.898 times 10 to the power negative 3 metres kelvin (m K). Note: the unit m K means metres times kelvin, not millikelvin. Rearranged: lambda max equals 2.898 times 10 to the power negative 3 divided by T. As temperature increases, peak wavelength decreases (shorter wavelength, higher frequency, higher energy photons), consistent with hotter objects appearing bluer. APPLICATIONS. Wien's law can be used to estimate the surface temperature of stars by measuring their peak output wavelength. The Sun's peak wavelength is approximately 500 nm, giving T equals 2.898 times 10 to the power negative 3 divided by 500 times 10 to the power negative 9 equals 5796 K, consistent with the Sun's surface temperature of about 5800 K. Betelgeuse, the red supergiant in Orion, has a peak wavelength of 9.35 times 10 to the power negative 7 metres, giving T equals 2.898 times 10 to the power negative 3 divided by 9.35 times 10 to the power negative 7 equals 3100 K. Wien's law and the Stefan-Boltzmann law together allow us to determine the size and temperature of stars from the electromagnetic radiation they emit.

subject: Physics
prerequisite: Stefan-Boltzmann law, inverse-square law, surface area
keywords: I = L divided by 4 pi d squared
content: INTENSITY AND LUMINOSITY. Luminosity L is the total power output of a star, i.e. the total energy radiated per second in all directions. It is measured in watts. Intensity I is the power received per unit area at a given distance from the star. Its unit is watts per metre squared (W per m squared). If light is emitted uniformly in all directions from a point source, it spreads out over the surface of an ever-expanding sphere. The surface area of a sphere of radius d is 4 pi d squared, so the intensity at distance d is: I equals L divided by 4 pi d squared. This follows the inverse-square law: doubling the distance d reduces the intensity to one quarter of its original value. FINDING DISTANCES TO STARS. If the luminosity L of a star is known (for example, if it is a standard candle), and the intensity I is measured on Earth, the distance d can be found by rearranging: d squared equals L divided by 4 pi times I. WORKED EXAMPLE. The Sun has luminosity L equals 3.8 times 10 to the power 26 W. The Earth-Sun distance d equals 1.5 times 10 to the power 11 m. I equals L divided by 4 pi d squared equals 3.8 times 10 to the power 26 divided by 4 pi times (1.5 times 10 to the power 11) squared equals 1347 W per m squared, approximately equal to 1350 W per m squared (the solar constant).

subject: Physics
prerequisite: Trigonometry, small angle approximation, electromagnetic radiation
content: TRIGONOMETRIC PARALLAX. Parallax is the apparent change of position of a nearby star against the background of more distant stars, caused by the Earth's motion around the Sun. As the Earth orbits the Sun, a nearby star appears to shift its position relative to distant background stars. This effect is measured by the parallax angle theta. Method: Measure the angle to a nearby star from two positions of the Earth separated by six months (opposite sides of the Earth's orbit). The angle between these two measurements is twice theta (where theta is the parallax angle). The greater the parallax angle, the closer the star. Using the small-angle approximation (tan theta approximately equals theta for small theta in radians): d equals r divided by theta, where r is the Earth-Sun distance (1 AU) and theta is the parallax angle in radians. DISTANCE UNITS. Astronomical Unit (AU): the average distance between the centres of the Earth and Sun. 1 AU equals 1.5 times 10 to the power 11 metres. Parsec (pc): the distance at which the parallax angle equals 1 arcsecond (1/3600th of a degree). 1 pc equals 2.06 times 10 to the power 5 AU equals 3.09 times 10 to the power 16 metres equals 3.26 light years. If the parallax angle theta is measured in arcseconds, then d in parsecs equals 1 divided by theta. Light year (ly): the distance light travels in one year in a vacuum. 1 ly equals 9.46 times 10 to the power 15 metres. LIMITATION: Trigonometric parallax is only accurate for nearby stars (up to about 100 pc for ground-based telescopes). Beyond this, the parallax angle becomes too small to measure accurately. The Gaia space telescope can measure parallax accurately out to about 40,000 pc (40 kpc).

subject: Physics
keywords: d equals square root of L divided by 4 pi I
content: STANDARD CANDLES. Standard candles are astronomical objects of known luminosity. If the luminosity L of an object is known, and its intensity I is measured on Earth, the distance d can be calculated from the inverse square law: d equals the square root of L divided by 4 pi times I. CEPHEID VARIABLE STARS. Henrietta Leavitt discovered in the early 20th century that Cepheid variable stars — which pulsate in brightness with a regular period — obey a period-luminosity relationship: the longer the oscillation period, the greater the luminosity. By measuring the period of a Cepheid variable, its luminosity can be determined. Then, measuring the intensity of light received on Earth and applying the inverse square law gives the distance to that star (and hence to its host galaxy). This technique works out to about 40 million parsecs, making Cepheid variables one of the most important distance indicators in cosmology. TYPE IA SUPERNOVAE. Type Ia supernovae always explode with approximately the same peak luminosity (about 10 billion times the luminosity of the Sun), making them excellent standard candles for measuring distances to very distant galaxies. By comparing the observed intensity of a Type Ia supernova with its known luminosity, distances of billions of parsecs can be estimated. TEMPERATURE-LUMINOSITY RELATIONSHIP. Main sequence stars of a known spectral class (determined from their absorption line spectrum) have a known luminosity (read from the HR diagram). This gives a third type of standard candle for determining stellar distances.

subject: Physics
prerequisite: Stefan-Boltzmann law, Wien's law, black body radiation
content: HERTZSPRUNG-RUSSELL DIAGRAM AND STELLAR CLASSIFICATION. Stars are classified into spectral classes based on their surface temperature. The spectral classes in order from hottest to coolest are O, B, A, F, G, K, M. A useful mnemonic is: Only Brilliant Astronomers Fix Great Kinematic Models. Spectral class O: blue, temperature 25000 to 50000 K. Spectral class B: blue, temperature 11000 to 25000 K. Spectral class A: blue-white, temperature 7500 to 11000 K. Spectral class F: white, temperature 6000 to 7500 K. Spectral class G: yellow-white, temperature 5000 to 6000 K. The Sun is class G. Spectral class K: orange, temperature 3500 to 5000 K. Spectral class M: red, temperature below 3500 K. THE HERTZSPRUNG-RUSSELL DIAGRAM. The HR diagram is a scatter plot of stellar luminosity against surface temperature. Temperature increases to the left on the horizontal axis. Important regions: Main sequence: a diagonal band running from hot, luminous stars (top left) to cool, dim stars (bottom right). Most stars spend most of their lifetime on the main sequence. Giants: luminous but cooler stars, located to the upper right. Supergiants: the most luminous stars, at the very top of the diagram. White dwarfs: hot but dim, located at the lower left. Using the Stefan-Boltzmann law L equals sigma times 4 pi r squared times T to the power 4, stars of the same luminosity but different temperatures have different radii. Stars to the right of the main sequence at the same luminosity must be larger.

subject: Physics
topic: 14. Stellar Evolution — Life Cycle of Stars
prerequisite: HR diagram, nuclear fusion, gravitational fields
content: STELLAR EVOLUTION — THE LIFE CYCLE OF STARS. The life cycle of a star depends primarily on its initial mass. STAGE 1: PROTOSTAR. All stars begin as clouds of gas and dust called nebulae. Fragments of the nebula have varying masses and clump together under gravity. As the clump rotates, conservation of angular momentum causes it to spin faster and contract, forming a denser, hotter centre called a protostar. STAGE 2: MAIN SEQUENCE. As a protostar contracts, its core temperature rises until nuclear fusion begins, fusing hydrogen nuclei into helium. The outward radiation pressure from fusion balances the inward gravitational force (hydrostatic equilibrium), making the star stable. Greater mass means shorter main sequence lifetime, as fuel is consumed faster. The Sun will remain on the main sequence for about 10 billion years in total. STAGE 3A: RED GIANT (for stars less than about 3 solar masses). Once hydrogen runs out in the core, the core contracts and heats up, and the outer layers expand and cool, making the star a red giant. Helium fusion begins, producing heavier elements such as carbon and oxygen. STAGE 4A: WHITE DWARF AND BLACK DWARF (less than 1.4 solar masses). The outer layers are expelled as a planetary nebula. The core contracts to form a white dwarf (very hot, very dense, Earth-sized). Over billions of years, the white dwarf cools to become a black dwarf (theoretical). STAGE 3B: RED SUPERGIANT (more than 3 solar masses). High-mass stars undergo the same initial evolution as red giants but on a larger scale, fusing heavier elements up to iron. STAGE 4B: SUPERNOVA (more than 1.4 solar masses). When fusion can no longer be sustained, the core collapses suddenly and becomes rigid. The outer layers rebound off the core in a huge shockwave called a supernova explosion, which fuses elements heavier than iron and flings them into space. STAGE 5: NEUTRON STAR (1.4 to 3 solar masses remaining after supernova). Gravity is so strong it forces protons and electrons together to form neutrons. The resulting object is incredibly dense (a teaspoon has mass of billions of tonnes). STAGE 6: BLACK HOLE (more than 3 solar masses remaining after supernova). The core collapses further until the gravitational pull is so strong that not even light can escape.

subject: Physics
topic: 15. The Doppler Effect and Cosmological Redshift
prerequisite: Wave properties, electromagnetic spectrum, speed of light
keywords: z = delta lambda divided by lambda
content: THE DOPPLER EFFECT AND COSMOLOGICAL REDSHIFT. The Doppler effect occurs when a wave source is moving relative to an observer. The observed wavelength (and frequency) of the wave is altered. If the source moves away from the observer: wavelength increases (redshift). If the source moves towards the observer: wavelength decreases (blueshift). For light from stars and galaxies: astronomers observed in the 1920s that the spectra of distant galaxies are shifted towards the red end of the spectrum — redshift. This means the galaxies are moving away from us. MEASURING REDSHIFT. The redshift parameter z is defined as: z equals delta lambda divided by lambda, which is approximately equal to delta f divided by f, which is approximately equal to v divided by c, where delta lambda is the change in wavelength (observed minus emitted), lambda is the emitted wavelength, delta f is the change in frequency, f is the emitted frequency, v is the recession velocity of the source, and c is the speed of light equal to 3.0 times 10 to the power 8 metres per second. This approximation holds for v much less than c (non-relativistic speeds). WORKED EXAMPLE. A hydrogen spectral line has an emitted wavelength of 656.285 nm. In the spectrum of a distant star, the same line is observed at 656.315 nm. Delta lambda equals 656.315 minus 656.285 equals 0.030 nm. v equals c times delta lambda divided by lambda equals 3.0 times 10 to the power 8 times 0.030 divided by 656.285 equals 1.37 times 10 to the power 4 m per s equals 13.7 km per s. The star is moving away from Earth at about 13.7 kilometres per second.

subject: Physics
topic: 16. Hubble's Law and the Expanding Universe
prerequisite: Doppler effect, redshift, distance measurement methods
content: HUBBLE'S LAW AND THE EXPANDING UNIVERSE. In 1929, Edwin Hubble published the finding that the red shift of a galaxy is proportional to its distance — the further a galaxy is, the faster it is moving away from us. This implies the Universe is expanding. HUBBLE'S LAW: v equals H0 times d, where v is the recession velocity of the galaxy in kilometres per second, d is the distance to the galaxy in megaparsecs (Mpc), and H0 is the Hubble constant (approximately 70.9 km per second per Mpc). In SI units: H0 approximately equals 2.29 times 10 to the power negative 18 per second. AGE OF THE UNIVERSE. If we assume the universe has been expanding at a constant rate, then time equals distance divided by velocity. Since v equals H0 times d: T0 equals d divided by v equals 1 divided by H0. T0 equals 1 divided by 2.29 times 10 to the power negative 18 equals 4.37 times 10 to the power 17 seconds equals approximately 13.8 billion years. This is the estimated age of the Universe from Hubble's law. UNCERTAINTY IN H0. The Hubble constant has been measured by different methods and gives values ranging from about 67 to 73 km per second per Mpc, leading to uncertainty in the age of the Universe (roughly 10 to 20 billion years range). The Gaia satellite is improving the accuracy of H0. EVIDENCE FOR EXPANSION. Almost all galaxies show redshift, indicating they are all moving away from each other. This is consistent with the Big Bang theory: the Universe began from a single point and has been expanding ever since.

subject: Physics
topic: 17. The Fate of the Universe: Dark Matter and Dark Energy
prerequisite: Hubble's law, gravitational fields, Newton's law of gravitation
content: THE FATE OF THE UNIVERSE: DARK MATTER AND DARK ENERGY. CRITICAL DENSITY AND THE FATE OF EXPANSION. The future of the Universe depends on its average density of matter. Critical density: if the mean density of the Universe exceeds the critical density, gravity will eventually halt the expansion and the Universe will collapse in a Big Crunch. If density is below critical: the Universe expands forever (open universe). If density equals critical: the Universe expands but slows to a stop in infinite time (flat universe). DARK MATTER. In the 1960s and 1970s, Vera Rubin found that stars in galaxies rotate at approximately the same orbital speed regardless of their distance from the galactic centre. This contradicts Newton's law: if all mass is in the visible centre, outer stars should orbit more slowly (as outer planets in the solar system do). The only explanation is that there is a large amount of invisible (dark) matter distributed throughout the galaxy providing extra gravitational force. Dark matter makes up about 26.8 percent of the Universe's total energy content. Its nature is unknown — candidates include WIMPs (weakly interacting massive particles) and primordial black holes. GRAVITATIONAL LENSING. Einstein's theory of general relativity predicts that massive objects curve spacetime, bending the path of light passing nearby. This gravitational lensing has been observed around galaxy clusters, providing independent evidence for dark matter: the observed lensing is stronger than expected from visible matter alone. DARK ENERGY. Observations of Type Ia supernovae in the late 1990s showed that the Universe's expansion is actually accelerating — not slowing down as expected if gravity were the only force. This acceleration is attributed to dark energy, a mysterious form of energy that permeates all of space and acts against gravity. Dark energy makes up approximately 68.3 percent of the total energy content of the Universe. Ordinary visible matter makes up only about 4.9 percent. CURRENT UNDERSTANDING: Dark matter provides extra gravitational force in galaxies; dark energy drives the accelerating expansion of the Universe. Both remain deeply mysterious and are active areas of research.
